Use when a project has no established working style yet, or it exhibits a facet no pack covers — during bootstrap of a fresh/empty repo, or on an uplevel request.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- single-branch-status: Assess one branch's landed status — merged, already-in-main, superseded, orphaned, or genuine unmerged work — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single branch is safe to delete, judging by content not the ref's name (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-branches task hands you branches to assess).
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose
2	
3	Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson and then runs this same skill over its **own** additions before landing them, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted — and that has already survived at least one of those upgrade passes.
4	
5	**Weekly, deliberately.** Fresh prose is handled the night it is written, so what reaches this sweep is a slow-moving corpus; a daily re-read of it spent an opus dispatch and an owner-gated PR on a backlog that had not changed.
6	
7	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
8	
9	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).
10	
11	## The method lives in the skill
12	
13	The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.
14	
15	## What a run does
16	
17	1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that govern **how we work** (not what the product does — see the skill's first gate), that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert), and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
18	2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Then apply the skill's **deletion test** to the prose the check now stands beside — a paragraph the check fully covers is deleted whole, never trimmed.
19	3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
20	4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".
21	
22	## What this task must never do
23	
24	- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
25	- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
26	- **Never convert a statement of what the product does** — a rule asserting which entities exist, what a surface renders, or that a feature's parts are wired together is a **requirement**, and belongs in the project's executable spec and the suite that proves it. Such a rule is testable, so it passes the check-the-world test on its own; the skill's first gate is what stops it. Found in pack prose it is already mis-homed — leave it and log it, never cement it as a check.
27	- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
28	- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.
29

1	---
2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs: prose that is always-testable but was never converted
9	becomes a check, so the packs keep shedding context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is
10	first learned.
11	
12	## Two callers, differing only in scope
13	
14	- **The upgrade pass**, as the last step of a
15	  [growth-extract](../../tasks/growth-extract/task.md) run: the scope is the prose **that run just
16	  wrote**. Extraction already descends the promotion ladder per lesson, but a lesson written as prose
17	  under time pressure is exactly where a convertible rule hides, so it gets asked once more before the
18	  PR opens. Never widen from here into the standing backlog.
19	- **The weekly [prose-to-checks-sweep](../../tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)**: the scope is the
20	  **standing backlog** — everything under the pack paths configured for this repo, which the task
21	  passes in its Context. A consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by
22	  default — projects don't improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core
23	  `packs/`. Read the prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them).
24	
25	Plus on demand, when someone asks. Either way: never edit a read-only mounted canon pack under
26	`.claudinite/shared/`. Everything below is identical for both callers.
27	
28	## First gate — a working rule, not a product statement
29	
30	Before asking whether a rule is *testable*, ask whether it belongs to a pack at all: **does it govern
31	how we work, or state what the product does?** A pack — canon or local — homes the conventions,
32	gotchas and review discipline that recur across tasks whatever the feature happens to be. A rule
33	asserting which entities exist, what a surface must render, or that a feature's parts are wired to
34	each other is a **requirement**; its home is the project's executable spec and the suite that proves
35	it (the full rule lives in
36	[generate-project-instructions](../generate-project-instructions/SKILL.md)).
37	
38	This gate comes **first** because product statements sail through the check-the-world test below —
39	"this module must export `X`" has an obvious static signature. Converting one splits a feature's
40	definition across two systems and lands half of it in the one no test of the product ever reads.
41	Load-bearingness is not the test: a real gap in product coverage is a *requirements* gap.
42	
43	A product statement already sitting in pack prose is mis-homed, and a sweep is not the place to
44	re-home it. **Leave the prose and log it** as a mis-homed rule, the same way an un-checkable
45	candidate is logged — never cement it as a check.
46	
47	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
48	
49	For each rule that cleared the gate, ask the one question from
50	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
51	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
52	
53	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
54	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
55	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
56	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
57	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
58	
59	**A static signature is necessary, not sufficient.** Both shapes the working-discipline rules bar
60	— a rule that pins today's code in place, and one derivable from the product's requirements —
61	answer *yes* here, so screen every candidate against that bar before converting it. Leave either
62	where it is; routing a requirement to the spec and its suite is its own change, not this sweep's.
63	
64	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
65	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
66	
67	## How to convert one
68	
69	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
70	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
71	
72	> **The upgrade-pass caller lands inside growth-extract's own PR**, which auto-merges after CI — so the
73	> see-it-fail fixture is the only gate a converted check gets there. Convert only what you can prove;
74	> anything shakier stays prose and waits for the weekly sweep's reviewed PR.
75	
76	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
77	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
78	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
79	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
80	   doesn't ship.
81	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
82	   directional by kind.
83	4. **Delete the prose the check now covers** — whole, never trimmed. The deletion test below is
84	   how you decide which paragraphs those are.
85	
86	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
87	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
88	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
89	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
90	check to the same fixture bar.
91	
92	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
93	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
94	
95	## Coming out: the deletion test
96	
97	Coming out of a conversion, apply the **deletion test**: prose a mechanism fully covers is
98	deleted, never trimmed. Ask it of every paragraph standing beside a landed check — *with this
99	paragraph gone, would the check still catch every violation it describes **and** tell the agent
100	how to fix it?* If yes, it is redundant: delete it whole. The check's failure message is where
101	the rule lives now and its header comment is where the rationale lives, so a paragraph restating
102	either pays twice and is the drift trap waiting to spring.
103	
104	Before concluding prose is the only carrier, look at the pack's **skills** too — an
105	activity-scoped skill often already holds the map a rule is repeating. Keep only what no artifact
106	carries.
107	
108	The test **discriminates** rather than just deleting: a paragraph stays whole whenever it carries
109	something the check does not — a second rule in the same breath, an exemption the check can't
110	encode, a value the check can't judge, or a remedy the finding's own `fix` line never states
111	(a finding renders `what` / `why` / `fix` / `doc`, never the rule's `description`, so a remedy
112	that lives only in the description is not carried). Two worked calls: an `npm test` invariant
113	went entirely — the check caught it and the testing-guide skill already listed the suites —
114	while an `extension-test/` mirror bullet stayed, because the check beside it enforced only the
115	`package.json` list's sync with the tree and never the mirror convention itself.
116	
117	Whether a check covers a rule is a judgment about meaning, so this test is applied by a
118	**reader**, not mechanized.
119	
120	## Bounds
121	
122	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
123	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
124	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — the deletion test is only ever asked of a rule a
125	  *landed* check now enforces.
126	- Run the suite and the sweep green before the PR goes up, and never push to `main` directly. The
127	  sweep opens its own PR for the owner's approval; the upgrade pass adds its conversion to the
128	  growth-extract PR already being opened, and opens none of its own.

1	# Checks — deterministic enforcement of the corpus (design)
2	
3	> **Status: implemented** (issue #127, #131). The runner, the baseline + technology packs, Stop
4	> hook, PreToolUse guard, and the pack-prose loader are live; the corpus is reorganized into
5	> `packs/` (prose + checks, active by declaration) and `skills/` (activity-scoped procedures).
6	> This doc is the rationale and the ongoing design record. The per-rule audit lives in
7	> [docs/conversion-inventory.md](../../docs/conversion-inventory.md).
8	
9	## The problem
10	
11	The corpus enforces style/practice rules as instructions. Instructions have three standing costs:
12	
13	1. **Context** — the always-on baseline loads every session whether or not it's needed, and
14	   adherence degrades as loaded context grows.
15	2. **Silent trigger failure** — soft-loaded docs depend on the agent following their trigger
16	   ("read filePlacement.md before placing a file"), which is itself instruction-following that
17	   fails silently. A rule the agent didn't read can't help.
18	3. **Invisible obsolescence** — a rule a newer Claude Code follows by default keeps costing
19	   tokens and attention forever; nothing measures that it stopped earning its place.
20	
21	A deterministic check inverts all three: it costs zero context until violated, fires whether or
22	not anything was read, and its firing history is measurable — a check that never fails is
23	evidence its rule can retire.
24	
25	## Why this is the right mechanism
26	
27	Anthropic's published guidance says this directly: hooks exist to provide "deterministic control
28	… ensuring certain actions always happen rather than relying on the LLM to choose to run them"
29	(hooks guide); CLAUDE.md is "context, not enforced" (memory doc); and the core best-practice is
30	"give Claude a check it can run … Claude does the work, runs the check, reads the result, and
31	iterates until the check passes" (best practices). The corpus already states the principle in
32	an agent-practices skill: *"Prose is a request; the
33	post-hoc diff check is the guarantee."* This design scales that sentence up.
34	
35	## What converts — and what doesn't
36	
37	An instruction leaves context only when a deterministic mechanism can carry it. Four targets,
38	picked per rule:
39	
40	| Mechanism | Fits when | Examples from the corpus |
41	|---|---|---|
42	| **Post-hoc check** (this system) | The rule constrains the *state of the repo* after work | file placement, dangling references, workflow lint, lifecycle compliance |
43	| **PreToolUse hook** | The action must be blocked *before* it runs | never delete a remote branch; don't `issue_write`-overwrite an issue body |
44	| **Skill / script** | A *procedure* or *knowledge* with a nameable (or path-scoped) trigger | the merge recipe; the lessons pass; the technology gotcha files |
45	| **Platform setting** | The platform enforces it outright, for free | squash-only merges; branch protection |
46	
47	Two classes deliberately **stay as instructions**:
48	
49	- **Process/judgment rules** — problem-first consensus, bug investigation method, naming
50	  quality. They shape work *in flight* and leave no artifact a check can inspect. Converting
51	  them post-hoc would also catch violations only after the expensive rework they exist to
52	  prevent.
53	- **Platform-gotcha knowledge** (`technologies/`) — split **per gotcha**, by whether the bad
54	  pattern has a *static signature in the artifact*. Where it does, it converts to a tech-pack
55	  check — a SAM `Handler` still carrying the entry's subdirectory under an esbuild build, an
56	  esbuild declared in `devDependencies`, a `SetIcon({path: …})`, a CloudFront custom
57	  origin-request policy listing `Authorization` — and the agent never needs to know the gotcha
58	  in advance: writing the bad pattern fails the check in the same session, moving discovery
59	  from runtime (often the first deploy or invoke) to write-time, with the gotcha's teaching in
60	  the failure message. Only the signature-less residue stays as skill knowledge: runtime
61	  divergence invisible in the artifact (jsdom *behaving* unlike Chrome, CORS being decided
62	  server-side) and diagnostic know-how. The release pack's **contract** is the
63	  largest signature-rich case — a conformance suite waiting to be written.
64	
65	## Architecture
66	
67	```
68	packs/                        # the mounted corpus: prose + checks, active by declaration
69	  registry.mjs                #   structural discovery — any packs/<name>/pack.mjs is a pack
70	  load-active-prose.mjs       #   SessionStart hook: emits active packs' RULES.md
71	  <baseline>/                 #   the baseline: RULES.md + the core checks (declared like any pack)
72	  <technology>/               #   coding gotchas (RULES.md, prose only)
73	  <technology>-release/       #   RELEASE.md (standard) + stubs + conformance checks (opt-in)
74	  <technology>/               #   the workflow lints (no prose)
75	  <technology>/  <technology>/  …      # more prose-only tech packs
76	  <project-class>/            #   a project-class pack (prose-only, declared)
77	checks/                       # the ENGINE only (runs the packs' checks)
78	  run.mjs                     #   dependency-free Node CLI
79	  lib/                        #   git diff scoping, findings format, markdown + manifest helpers
80	  stop-hook.mjs               #   blocks the agent's stop on blocking findings
81	  pretooluse-guard.mjs        #   blocks forbidden actions before they run
82	  test/                       #   fixtures (scratch git repos), red-first
83	packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/   # activity-scoped procedures, bundled in their owning pack
84	  checks.mjs                  #   the test-the-world checks that validate this skill's action
85	```
86	
87	**Skill-owned checks.** A skill defines the performance of an *action*; the test-the-world
88	check that validates that action's result belongs **beside the SKILL.md that defines it**, not
89	in a pack that owns none of the context. So a skill may carry its own checks — the
90	`routine-structure` check lives in its owning skill's folder, next to the routine-authoring
91	prose it enforces, with its test co-located too. A skill lives inside its owning pack
92	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/` — #385), so discovery IS the pack registry: any bundled skill's
93	`checks.mjs` (default export = an array of rules) is gathered onto the pack (`skillChecks`) and
94	runs when the pack is active. The pack gate only says the project opted into the pack — not
95	that this skill's action ever happened in this repo — so a skill check's `run` must still
96	**detect relevance first, cheaply and specifically, and return `[]` when
97	the artifact is absent** (`routine-structure` keys off a `routine.md` existing before it asserts
98	anything). Get that wrong and the check fires false findings on every unrelated repo the corpus
99	is mounted in. Reserve skill checks for the world-state a skill's action leaves behind; a rule
100	with no skill to anchor it stays a baseline check.
101	
102	**Where a check goes — the litmus test.** Classify by what the checked *artifact* is, not by
103	which doc teaches the fix (the `doc` pointer is where you *learn* the remedy — most baseline
104	checks point at a skill, so it is **not** the classifier):
105	
106	- present in ~every repo (markdown links, file layout, the root `CLAUDE.md`, git history, a
107	  branch's issue reference) → a **baseline** check;
108	- present only when a declared **technology** is (a workflow, a SAM template, the release
109	  stubs) → a **technology-pack** check, whose relevance is gated by declaration;
110	- present **only because one skill's discrete action created it** (a routine folder, from
111	  authoring a routine) → a **skill** check.
112	
113	Only the third — *the artifact would not exist had the action never run* — earns a home in the
114	skill. `routine-structure` is the sole current case: a routine folder exists only because
115	someone authored a routine. `squash-merge-history` points at the merge skill but stays
116	in the baseline, because git history exists in every repo and is disturbed by any merge, not only that
117	skill's action; `claude-md-length`, `generated-merge-driver`, and the placement check likewise
118	inspect artifacts every repo has, so they stay in the baseline despite naming a skill in `doc`.
119	
120	**Not every pack-machinery concern is a check.** The `.claudinite-checks.json` *settings* are
121	validated when the file loads, not by a conformance rule: malformed JSON, an unknown property,
122	and an unknown pack name are equally settings errors, surfaced by the runner as blocking `config`
123	findings. A pack's `marker` only *suspects* the pack is wanted — whether to declare it is the
124	project's call — so nothing checks that a declared pack carries its marker, or that a marker's
125	pack is declared. Pack **dependencies** (`requires`) are likewise resolved when the declaration is
126	*written* — bootstrap `--init` and the baselining backfill run `resolveDeclaredPacks` to pull each
127	declared pack's transitive `requires` into the file, materializing the prerequisite (like
128	the baseline) rather than nagging at every Stop. A materialized dependency is written as
129	`{ "id": ..., "via": [...] }` — `via` naming the declared packs that require it — so the file
130	itself records why the dependency is there.
131	
132	**Runner contract.** `node .claudinite/checks/run.js`. Dependency-free Node — no `npm install`
133	step exists on the tarball mount, and the corpus's own "earn each dependency" rule applies to
134	us first. Exit 0 = clean, exit 1 = blocking findings. The default scope is the **whole repo**:
135	on a text corpus the full sweep costs milliseconds, and only full scope sees cross-file
136	breakage — a change in one file dangling a reference in an unchanged one. The steady state is
137	a repo at zero findings (or reviewed acceptances), held there by every run. `--changed`
138	(diff vs the merge-base with main) exists only as a transitional aid while adopting a repo
139	that carries a backlog — it is not the enforcement default. (Rules that are inherently about
140	the *delta* — new suppression markers, commits referencing an issue — diff against the
141	merge-base in either scope.)
142	
143	**Pack selection: declared for deterministic execution, fingerprinted against drift.** The
144	packs a project runs are **pinned in `.claudinite-checks.json`**
145	(`"packs": ["baseline", "a-technology-pack", "a-release-pack"]`; no pack runs
146	undeclared — the baseline too is declared explicitly, seeded by bootstrap).
147	Execution is a closed, declared set: every rule in a declared pack
148	runs when its scope's surface runs — the work rules at the Stop hook, the world rules in the
149	test/CI flow — with no inference at execution time, so "the
150	project uses technology X" deterministically implies "every X check ran." Bootstrap writes the
151	initial declaration from the repo's fingerprint — a pack's `detect` marker (`.github/workflows/`
152	→ a workflow-lint pack; a `manifest.json` with `manifest_version` → the extension packs; the
153	release-workflow `name:`s → the conformance suite) seeds it at `--init`. But a marker only
154	*suspects* a pack is wanted: from then on the declaration is authoritative, and whether to add a
155	newly adopted technology's pack, or drop one whose technology has left, is the **project's** call
156	— the checker never second-guesses it. What *is* enforced is settings **validity**: an unknown
157	pack name, an unknown property, or malformed JSON is caught when the file loads
158	(`loadConfig` + the runner) and surfaced as a blocking `config` error — a wrong pack name is as
159	much a settings error as bad JSON. `.claudinite-checks.json` additionally holds per-rule
160	**overrides** and **acceptances** — at the top level for project-wide decisions, or on a pack's
161	own entry for the ones that pack's declaration motivates (see engine/checks/README.md).
162	
163	A declared id may name a **canon** pack or one of the repo's **own local packs**
164	(`.claudinite/local_packs/<id>/` — the project's tracked, project-specific packs, discovered from
165	the repo's own tree alongside the mounted canon; canonically declared by the namespaced token
166	`local_packs/<id>`, the bare id accepted while the fleet migrates — see engine/checks/README.md). Both
167	are the same closed-declared-set execution;
168	`knownIds` spans both, so a local id is valid, not an unknown-pack error, while a broken or
169	id-colliding local `pack.mjs` is surfaced as a blocking `config` finding rather than silently
170	dropping the pack's checks. A local pack's checks run when it is declared, exactly like a canon
171	pack's; this is where a project's *own* deterministic rules live (the checks-over-prose economy,
172	applied at the project's level) instead of always-loaded prose.
173	
174	**Acceptances are the escape hatch — deterministic and reviewable.** Rules with judgment
175	exemptions (a placement rule's "deliberate cross-cutting concern") need a way to say "yes, on
176	purpose" that isn't a fight with the hook: a per-finding `accept` entry with a mandatory reason
177	string, keyed by rule id + path. It lands in the diff like any code, so the *decision* gets
178	reviewed once instead of re-litigated every session. An acceptance a pack's adoption forces
179	lives on that pack's `packs` entry, so its provenance — which declaration required which
180	exception — is the file's own structure.
181	
182	An acceptance is a **check-the-world** instrument: a persistent, committed exemption a future
183	sweep keeps re-finding and must be told to ignore. It is the wrong tool for a **check-the-work**
184	finding — a conversation- or branch-scoped rule (e.g. `feature-requirements-first`) whose finding
185	a fresh session wouldn't even re-raise; accepting one leaves a permanent suppression for a
186	one-session artifact. Author a check-the-work rule to be **satisfiable by fixing the work, or to
187	self-skip** when its precondition isn't met (the spec it enforces against isn't in the repo, say):
188	a finding no correct work can clear forces the wrong remedy — an accept, or a post-hoc rebase —
189	so it's a bug in the rule, not a candidate for an acceptance.
190	
191	And when a rule mandates an **ordering** — X must happen before Y — it ships with a
192	check-the-work verification of that order, judged on the surface where the order is visible:
193	the conversation transcript (`feature-requirements-first`'s comment-scoped doc-first ordering)
194	or the branch commit log (a rule-before-fix test asserting the outlawing commit is an ancestor
195	of the fixing one, `pack-independence`'s pattern). A stated ordering with no check-the-work
196	verifier is prose-only enforcement — exactly what this system exists to replace.
197	
198	**The finding is the instruction.** This is the context economy of the whole design: the rule's
199	teaching text moves out of always-loaded context and into the failure message, paying its token
200	cost only on violation, in the session that violated it, pointed at the exact spot. Every
201	finding carries: rule id, `file:line`, what's wrong, *why* (one line — the model generalizes
202	from motivation), the fix, and a doc pointer for depth.
203	
204	<example>
205	
206	```
207	reference-distance  src/report/render.js:12
208	  imports ../../util/dates.js at distance 4.
209	  Why: the folder tree should encode the dependency graph; far reaches make it lie.
210	  Fix: move dates.js next to its users, lift it to a common ancestor, or accept it
211	       in .claudinite-checks.json with a reason if it's a deliberate cross-cutting util.
212	  More: .claudinite/shared/packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md
213	```
214	
215	</example>
216	
217	## Enforcement wiring
218	
219	The two scopes fire at **different times**, because they answer different questions. The *work*
220	scope judges the change in front of the session and belongs on a per-turn hook; the *world* scope
221	is a whole-repo invariant assertion — the same shape as a test suite — and belongs wherever the
222	project runs its tests, not on every turn.
223	
224	**Work scope: a Stop hook is the guarantee; instructions are not.** Bootstrap registers one hook
225	in the consumer's `.claude/settings.json` (the same mechanism as the existing SessionStart hooks):
226	
227	1. The Stop hook fires when the agent finishes a turn.
228	2. It **fast-exits in milliseconds** when no tracked file differs from `main` — conversational
229	   turns cost nothing.
230	3. Otherwise it runs the **work** sweep (`check_the_work.mjs`, with the session transcript); on
231	   findings it exits 2 with them on stderr. Claude Code blocks the stop and feeds that text back
232	   to the agent, which fixes the violations **in the same session**. A clean run stops silently.
233	
234	Loop safety comes from convergence (fixed findings stop firing) plus Claude Code's own runaway
235	protection (it overrides a Stop hook after ~8 consecutive blocks).
236	
237	**World scope: wired into the project's test/CI flow (revises #385).** The whole-repo sweep runs
238	as its own step wherever the project runs its tests — a CI job, a `make test` target, an npm
239	script — invoked as the standalone `node .claudinite/shared/engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs`
240	command. It is deliberately **not** a language-specific test file (a `*.test.mjs` a Node runner
241	discovers): a Python/Rust/Go consumer's suite could not load one, and the sweep is the engine's
242	own always-vendored Node CLI, so it runs as a step in any flow regardless of the project's
243	language. Bootstrap wires this step during adoption, adding a minimal flow where the repo has
244	none. This **supersedes the original #385 decision** ("the Stop hook is the whole enforcement
245	surface; consumers ship no CI job"): the earlier design kept the world sweep on Stop to spare
246	consumers a CI setup, but running a whole-repo sweep every turn is work misplaced in time, and a
247	human editing on GitHub web (or any non-session tool) is now caught by the test/CI flow the
248	change lands through rather than by the next session's Stop.
249	
250	**The conversation surface (Stop hook only).** Some process rules leave their artifact not in
251	the repo but in the *session itself* — e.g. `comment-classification` (the reply to the owner's
252	latest comment must declare an explicit `Comment class:` line: the assessment stays judgment,
253	but that an assessment was made is checkable) and `feature-requirements-first` (a
254	feature-classified comment's doc-first ordering on the branch). The Stop hook is the one surface
255	that can carry these: Claude Code passes the hook `transcript_path` on stdin, the hook forwards
256	it as `--transcript`, and `ctx.conversation()` exposes the parsed session
257	([helpers/session-transcript.mjs](helpers/session-transcript.mjs)). Everywhere else — CI, a manual run — the transcript
258	is absent and these rules self-gate to `[]`, the same self-supplied relevance gate skill checks
259	use. Two scoping choices keep them convergent rather than nagging: only the *latest* owner
260	comment is judged (a transcript is append-only, so an old omission could never be fixed), and
261	the ordering rule scopes to commits after the comment's timestamp (earlier work on the branch is
262	never re-litigated). The Stop hook's clean fast path also means a purely conversational turn —
263	no tracked change vs the base — runs no checks at all, conversation rules included.
264	
265	**Prefer a platform setting when one exists — but never trust it.** Squash-only merging is a
266	GitHub repo setting; force-push protection is branch protection. The setting does the
267	*enforcing*, but it's configuration like any other: it can be off, get switched off, or be
268	bypassed, and nothing notices. So every setting rung pairs with a check that verifies it, in
269	order of strength:
270	
271	- **Effect check (preferred)** — offline and deterministic, it verifies the *outcome* the
272	  setting guarantees rather than the setting itself: squash-only ⇒ the change lands squashed,
273	  so its own commits carry no merge commit (`squash-merge-history` in the baseline pack). It
274	  is scoped to the work — the merge commits the current change introduces on HEAD's first-parent
275	  chain since the merge-base — not the repo's whole history: it catches the setting being off or
276	  bypassed *for this change* without re-auditing (and demanding acceptances for) legacy merges
277	  already on `main` that the work never touched. Testing the work, not the world, is what keeps
278	  the check from firing on every unrelated session.
279	
280	  **A work-scoped rule is only as honest as the ref it scopes against.** "Since the merge-base"
281	  is a correct definition that silently becomes a wrong verdict when the base ref is stale —
282	  a cloud session's clone freezes `origin/main` at container-creation time, so everything the
283	  base branch gained since then reads as introduced by the work, and a *blocking* rule starts
284	  reporting other people's merges on a branch that has none of its own. Two mechanisms keep the
285	  scope honest, both in `buildContext` rather than in any one rule: the base ref is refreshed
286	  before the merge-base is computed (best-effort, bounded, opt-out — [README](README.md)), and
287	  candidates are confirmed against the base ref itself, because `git merge-base` returns one of
288	  several equally-good answers on a criss-cross history and the one it picks can leave a merge
289	  that is already on the base branch inside the range. Scoping a delta rule is two jobs: pick
290	  the range, and make sure the range's endpoint is telling the truth.
291	- **Config check** — reads the setting via the platform API and fails when it's off. Needs a
292	  network-capable surface: rules carry a surface tag, the Stop hook runs only offline rules,
293	  CI runs what its repo token can read (e.g. the allow-merge-commit flags), and the fleet
294	  maintenance routine covers settings a repo token can't (e.g. branch protection). Follow-up
295	  work alongside the Phase 2 packs.
296	
297	## Governance
298	
299	- **A converted rule leaves its doc — deleted whole, not trimmed.** The check's failure message
300	  owns the rule now and its header comment owns the rationale, so the doc keeps only what neither
301	  carries: the judgment parts, the exemptions a check can't encode, the rules it doesn't reach.
302	  A paragraph restating a landed check's message or its rationale pays twice and springs the
303	  corpus's own drift trap (two sources of truth). The per-paragraph decision is the
304	  `prose-to-checks` skill's deletion test, applied by a reader.
305	- **Fail fast: a new check ships at its real severity — blocking for defect-kind rules.** A
306	  wrong blocking check surfaces in the very next session and gets fixed; an advisory false
307	  positive is noise nobody reads, so a burn-in stage never actually observes the precision it
308	  waits for. The escape hatches bound a bad check's blast radius: a reasoned acceptance, a
309	  severity override, and the Stop hook's own two-block release. `advisory` remains a per-rule
310	  **kind**, not a stage — for rules whose own semantics are directional (a placement rule's
311	  metric is "a direction, not a hard gate"), where a finding is a smell to judge, not a defect
312	  to fix. Revisit delayed adoption only if the fleet grows people who can be hurt by a wrong
313	  block.
314	- **Telemetry drives retirement.** The runner logs firings; the fleet-maintenance routine
315	  already reads every vendored repo and can report "rules that never fired in N days" —
316	  obsolescence made measurable, the property instructions never had.
317	
318	## Skills — the on-demand layer for what checks can't carry
319	
320	Checks carry the *enforceable* rules. Everything else that today rides on soft pointers —
321	procedures, task-gated practices, technology knowledge — moves to **Agent Skills**, a mechanism
322	the system doesn't use yet. The docs' own decision rule fits exactly: *"Create a skill when …
323	a section of CLAUDE.md has grown into a procedure rather than a fact"*, and knowledge-bearing
324	skills are explicitly endorsed (*"reference content adds knowledge … conventions, patterns,
325	style guides, domain knowledge"*). The official hook-vs-skill line mirrors this design's ladder:
326	*"Use a hook when the action must happen the same way every time … Use a skill when Claude
327	should decide how to apply the steps, or when the content is knowledge rather than a script."*
328	
329	**What a skill buys over a CLAUDE.md soft pointer.** The token economics are roughly neutral —
330	a skill's name + description sit in context every session (progressive disclosure: the body
331	loads only on invocation), about what an index line costs today. The real gain is **trigger
332	reliability**: today a `tasks/` doc helps only if the agent remembers to follow the index line
333	("read before writing a test") — an instruction-following step that fails silently. Skill
334	matching is harness-managed and trained-for, skills are user-invocable as `/name` too (manual
335	invocation is deterministic — it runs when typed), and technology skills can be
336	**`paths`-scoped** (glob frontmatter) so they surface exactly when the matching files are
337	touched — a structural trigger, not a remembered one.
338	
339	Be clear about what this is *not*: **model-invocation of a skill is still probabilistic** —
340	better odds than a soft pointer, never a guarantee. That is precisely why this design's
341	division of labor puts nothing that *must* happen on a skill: enforcement lives in hooks,
342	checks, and settings, which are deterministic by construction; skills carry only guidance whose
343	worst-case miss is today's status quo. In particular, check execution never depends on skill
344	routing — the Stop hook runs the declared packs whether or not any skill fired. The split is
345	therefore **per-rule, not per-doc**: a doc's enforceable rules go to a pack (which runs
346	unconditionally for every project that declares it), its judgment residue rides the skill, and
347	there is deliberately no one-to-one correspondence between an instruction file and a pack. Two documented limits
348	to respect: keep descriptions tight (the listing truncates them, and the description budget
349	scales with the context window — many verbose skills degrade matching), and keep each
350	`SKILL.md` body well under 500 lines.
351	
352	### The catalog
353	
354	There is no skill catalog (#385): a skill is its owning pack's content
355	(`<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`) — the pack's own README names what it bundles, and the
356	harness surfaces skills by their frontmatter descriptions, which is the routing.
357	
358	What stays always-loaded after this: a trimmed
359	baseline `RULES.md`, the judgment core of
360	the agent-practices skill (its trigger — "writing
361	code" — is near-universal, so a skill gains little; revisit with telemetry), and a much smaller
362	index. The routing index largely dissolves: routing *is what skill descriptions do natively*.
363	
364	### Delivery — incremental now, plugin end-state
365	
366	- **Now (works with both mount methods):** each skill is bundled in its owning pack
367	  (`<pack>/skills/<name>/`), and the SessionStart hook `engine/pack_loader/mount-skills.mjs`
368	  regenerates `.claude/skills/<name>` symlinks for the active packs' union each session —
369	  nothing committed (a committed link dangles on every plain checkout). Symlinked skill
370	  directories are documented, supported behavior, and skill changes are picked up live within
371	  a session — so mounts generated at session start still land, the same property the tarball
372	  sync populating their targets already relies on.
373	- **Later, maybe — Claudinite as a plugin (contingent on a spike).** A plugin is nothing
374	  exotic: a directory layout inside an ordinary git repo (`skills/`, `commands/`,
375	  `hooks/hooks.json`, a `plugin.json` manifest) plus a `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json` that
376	  lets the repo serve as its own catalog. **No publication to Anthropic** — any git repo works
377	  as a marketplace directly, and the repo may carry arbitrary other content alongside the
378	  plugin dirs, so Claudinite would remain exactly the freely-amended GitHub repo it is (growth
379	  PRs, this doc, everything — unchanged). The draw: plugins bundle precisely this design's
380	  pieces — skills, commands, and hooks (SessionStart, Stop, PreToolUse) with bundled scripts
381	  addressable via `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` — and a consumer repo can commit
382	  `extraKnownMarketplaces` + `enabledPlugins` in `.claude/settings.json` to enable it for
383	  everyone. **Why it is not the plan of record:** the docs leave the operational questions that
384	  matter most to this system unanswered — how promptly consumers receive updates (manual
385	  `/plugin marketplace update` is documented; session-start auto-refresh is not), whether
386	  web/cloud sessions load marketplace plugins at all, and whether plugin hooks behave
387	  identically to settings-registered ones. A daily-growth corpus lives or dies on update
388	  latency, and the current SessionStart tarball sync *guarantees* latest-`main` every session.
389	  So: phases 1–4 ship entirely on the existing mount + symlinks and depend on the plugin route
390	  for nothing; adopt it only if a Phase-5 spike proves same-day propagation, web support, and
391	  hook parity. (Also documented: a plugin cannot inject always-on CLAUDE.md-style prose, so the
392	  residual baseline keeps its `@`-import either way.)
393	
394	## Growth pipeline: checks-first promotion
395	
396	New lessons enter the canon through the growth lifecycle (extract → promote → dedup). Today
397	the promote step generalizes a lesson and routes it to a prose doc.
398	Under this design, **prose becomes the fallback, not the default** — the point of promotion is
399	to relieve every project's context, and a check relieves it completely while prose only
400	relocates it.
401	
402	**The promotion ladder.** Every lesson that clears the worthiness bar is triaged down the same
403	mechanism order as the conversion table above — the *first* rung that can carry it wins:
404	
405	1. **Platform setting** — the platform enforces it outright, always paired with the check
406	   that verifies it holds (effect check first, config check where a token can read it).
407	2. **PreToolUse hook** — a bad action to block before it runs.
408	3. **Post-hoc check** — a constraint on repo state.
409	4. **Skill** — a procedure or knowledge with a nameable trigger.
410	5. **Prose canon** — only for what none of the above can carry, and the landing **names its
411	   reason** (judgment / in-flight behavior / platform knowledge), logged per lesson in the
412	   promote tracking issue so conversion rates are auditable.
413	
414	Concretely, three growth docs change:
415	
416	- **`item-routing.md`** gains a step 0: *mechanism triage*
417	  before file routing. "Which doc owns this" is only asked for lessons that fall through to
418	  rung 5.
419	- **the promote task doc**: for a rung-3 lesson, the routine authors
420	  the check in the same PR — rule id, detection, the failure message (which *is* the
421	  generalized lesson text), **plus a fixture proving it fires** on a violating input and stays
422	  quiet on a clean one (see-it-fail applies to checks too). When it can't produce a confident
423	  detection + fixture, it lands the lesson as prose **and** opens a tagged conversion-backlog
424	  issue — a visible miss to sweep later, never a silently-shipped broken check.
425	- **the dedup task doc**: a canon **check** covers a local prose item the
426	  same way a canon line does — better, since the coverage is enforced rather than stated. The
427	  runner exposes the rule catalog machine-readably (`run.js --list`: rule id, description,
428	  failure message, doc pointer); dedup quotes a **rule id** where it today quotes a canon line.
429	  This answers the obvious worry — "the canon won't have the instruction, only a test": the
430	  check *carries* its instruction as data (its failure message), so dedup compares against the
431	  catalog exactly as it compares against prose today, and more mechanically, since rule ids are
432	  stable where prose wording drifts. The keep-test is unchanged: a local item that says *more*
433	  than the check detects (a stronger point about a narrower case) stays.
434	
435	Extract is untouched: project-local capture stays prose at the project's own level —
436	conversion is a promotion-time judgment, made once, centrally.
437	
438	## Phasing
439	
440	1. **Runner + Stop hook + first baseline checks** — reference-integrity, task-lifecycle,
441	   warning-suppression (blocking); the placement check (advisory by kind). Bootstrap gains the
442	   hook-registration step.
443	2. **a workflow-lint pack + a release-conformance pack**, piloted on one
444	   extension repo.
445	3. **Baseline restructure** — the first skills (a merge recipe, a lessons pass) + the
446	   squash-only setting; temporary-workarounds → PreToolUse hook; slim the converted docs and
447	   the index.
448	4. **Skills layer + growth pivot** — the rest of the corpus (practice + technology skills,
449	   symlink delivery in bootstrap), and the promotion ladder lands in
450	   the promote task doc,
451	   `item-routing.md`, and
452	   the dedup task doc.
453	5. **(Contingent) plugin packaging** — only after a spike proves same-day update propagation,
454	   web-session support, and hook parity; until then the mount + symlink delivery is the plan of
455	   record and nothing depends on this phase.
456	6. **(Deferred)** LLM-judge checks in CI for judgment rules (naming, comment quality) —
457	   possible, but nondeterministic and token-costly; revisit only after 1–4 prove out.

1	# Claudinite — the canon's own non-portable working rules
2	
3	This is the Claudinite home repo's own local pack: the capture surface for lessons that are
4	**specific to working on the canon itself** and would not make sense mounted into a consuming
5	project. Portable lessons — anything true for repos beyond this one — belong in the shared canon
6	under `packs/`/`skills/` instead (proposed by PR, or lifted by the promote stage).
7	
8	The growth lifecycle writes here automatically: the `growth-extract` daily task routes the canon's
9	own non-portable lessons — mined from repo activity and from captured conversations alike — into
10	this pack (each at the local promotion ladder's strongest mechanism — a check where the rule is deterministic, otherwise terse
11	prose below).
12	
13	## Standing owner decisions — settled, do not re-litigate
14	
15	- **`canon-curation` lives in `.claudinite/local/packs/`, not `packs/`** (owner decision,
16	  2026-07-19). The canon home's curation duties are Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite —
17	  project-specific content on the home's own capture surface. Do not propose moving it back, and
18	  do not describe the move as open or provisional.
19	- **Local-pack `run_daily` scheduling is ON — the fleet's default path** (same decision). The
20	  planner reads every member's local-pack daily descriptors by default; never reintroduce an
21	  "experimental / not enabled" framing or an opt-in seam for it.
22	- **Packs-tree segregation is barriers configuration only.** Any rule about what the `packs/`
23	  tree may reference is expressed by declaring/configuring the `barriers` pack (contributed
24	  edges, `siblings`/`scope` capabilities — extend barriers generically if a capability is
25	  missing). Never write standalone code that checks packs-tree segregation.
26	- **A `docs/<initiative>/DESIGN.md` records the mechanism only** (owner decision, 2026-07-23,
27	  #420). Status, phase tracking, in-flight-PR reconciliation and remaining work live in that
28	  initiative's tracking issue (task-prework → #394); a phased plan lives in the sibling
29	  `MIGRATION.md`. Don't reintroduce a status / open-questions / remaining-work section there.
30	- **Multi-session work hands off through the tracking issue, never a prepared prompt** (owner
31	  correction, 2026-07-23). The owner's opener is `continue work on #<n>`, so state not written
32	  into the issue is lost. Before ending a session on unfinished work, update the issue and let
33	  the session summary be a pointer to it — never compose a bespoke "pick up from here" prompt.
34	- **The canon never knows which repos consume it — fleet-wide aggregation is Sheepdog's domain**
35	  (owner correction, 2026-07-28, #520). Designing anything that spans repos, the tempting shape is
36	  a member list (or a "fleet" task) living in the canon. It doesn't go here: the canon carries only
37	  **mechanisms exercised on itself**, and the knowledge of *which* repos exist stays in the
38	  **Sheepdog** repo and its pack, which enumerates members at runtime from its own
39	  `.claudinite-checks.json` entry — exactly where `fleet-census` and `fleet-freshness` already keep
40	  it. So a cross-repo feature splits in two: a self-contained per-repo half in the canon, and the
41	  aggregation half as a Sheepdog fleet task. **No repo list exists anywhere in canon code** — and a
42	  derived fleet artifact lands in Sheepdog as a daily **auto-merged PR of a `GENERATED` file**,
43	  never a direct commit to its `main`.
44	- **A pack default stays in the pack — don't ask it at adoption, don't write it into a member's
45	  config** (owner ruling, 2026-07-28, #527/#528). An adoption question whose recommended answer is
46	  right for nearly everyone is "bad noise": it taxes every adopting repo to re-state the default,
47	  and materializing that answer into `.claudinite-checks.json` freezes a copy that then drifts from
48	  the pack and has to be migrated. Keep the default in the pack's own code, ask nothing, and let the
49	  rare project that wants to differ add the setting by hand. Read config as *optional* — an unset
50	  key means "the default", never "misconfigured" (`retention_days` unset is precisely why the
51	  growth-extract retention prune is skipped rather than failing).
52	
53	- **What Claudinite ships must run on the credentials and settings a member already has**
54	  (owner ruling, 2026-08-06). Requiring a member to flip a platform setting, or to provision a wider
55	  credential (a PAT, an app installation, a new secret), is a last resort — not because it is hard,
56	  but because it is per-repo manual work that reliably does not happen: the capability is then
57	  quietly dead in every repo nobody configured, indistinguishable from a Claudinite bug, while the
58	  automation's own report says nothing is wrong. Three members filed issues asking for the same
59	  Actions approval setting (ClaudiniteWebsite#95, EdFringeNow#205, TLDR#182); none was changed, and
60	  each repo's converge kept succeeding while its mount fell a day behind. Prefer the route that
61	  works with the Action's own `GITHUB_TOKEN` and stock configuration even when it is less direct,
62	  and where a platform behaviour blocks you, neutralise its *effect* rather than asking for the
63	  platform to be reconfigured. Where no such route exists — a capability the default credential
64	  cannot hold at all, which is why `FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN` is legitimate — take the requirement
65	  deliberately: name the exact scope, say why nothing weaker suffices, and have the automation
66	  report when it is missing rather than silently degrading.
67	
68	- **A change to what members receive is not verified until a member has received it — force that in
69	  the same session** (owner requirement, 2026-08-06: *"We're not waiting till tomorrow to see if
70	  something worked"*). Merging to canon is evidence about canon; the only thing that exercises a
71	  canon change end to end is a member's converge, and on a daily slot that is a day away — so a
72	  session that closes on "it reaches the fleet tonight" has shipped an unverified change and hands
73	  the owner a question they will ask anyway (asked five separate ways across 2026-08-05/06:
74	  *"Check status"*, *"Did the Sheepdog baselining work?"*, *"check now"*, *"How do you know 'the
75	  fleet is now fully on 076c029'?"*, and forced baselines appended to three consecutive `lgtm`s).
76	  After landing anything that alters what baselining delivers, drive Sheepdog's `fleet-baseline`
77	  workflow with `follow` and report what it did per member, unasked. Two corollaries. **A dispatch
78	  is not a result** — the API's 204 means queued. And **attaching a member repo to the session is a
79	  read you already have**, so attach the repos the verification needs rather than offering to: *"2
80	  of 11 members confirmed … say the word and I'll attach and verify"* bought a round-trip, one of
81	  four the owner spent that morning telling this session to attach repos.
82	
83	## Canon-specific gotchas
84	
85	- **Baselining backfill skips the home.** The nightly baselining that lands a `seededByDefault`
86	  pack (and canon-delivered declaration changes) on every member is gated `!isHome`, so the canon
87	  home is the one repo it never reaches: what the fleet receives automatically, this repo's own
88	  `.claudinite-checks.json` only ever gets by hand.
89	- **Pack discovery imports the whole pack tree eagerly — declaration is irrelevant.**
90	  `discoverPacks` imports every `packs/<name>/pack.mjs` on disk and `scanSkillChecks` imports
91	  every `<pack>/skills/<skill>/checks.mjs` beside it, *before* activation is consulted. So
92	  anything in that import graph loads in every repo under every declaration, and a module that is
93	  also a CLI entry point gets re-imported while it is still evaluating: a top-level `await` in its
94	  entry block then never settles and Node exits 13 having run nothing (#581 — `interview.mjs
95	  check` deadlocked fleet-wide, invisible because the SessionStart orchestrator's fail-soft reads
96	  it as a merely-absent note). Start the work *after* evaluation completes — `check(…).catch(…)`.
97	  Enforced by `pack-discovery-entry-await`; the corollary it can't check is to keep these modules
98	  import-light in the first place.
99	- **Green canon CI is not evidence about a consumer — the canon's own packs are always already
100	  migrated.** The one thing canon CI cannot exercise is what a canon change does to a repo on its
101	  *next* baselining, and every consumer-breaking change so far passed it cleanly: #555 (manifest
102	  became a closed vocabulary → 11 local packs across 10 repos silently stopped running their
103	  checks), #585 (PR-open status never read → 12 repos frozen two days while the run reported
104	  `ok`), #588 (auto-merge armed where no PR CI exists → a PR that never lands). All were invisible
105	  until a consumer ran. So when a change adds or requires a manifest field, moves a check's
106	  severity or id, or alters a vendored contract, say in the PR *which* consumer-side evidence
107	  carries it — a migration record, or a demonstration that an unmigrated member stays green — and
108	  never treat a green canon suite as that evidence (#592 tracks the missing gate).
109	- **A pack's `RULES.md` is injected into every session that declares the pack — an idea nobody can
110	  act on belongs in `docs/`, and a pack file must not link there.** Deferred directions, blocked
111	  proposals and status live in `docs/` (e.g. `docs/future-directions.md`) precisely because pack
112	  prose costs context in every consumer session. And the pointer cannot go the other way: `docs/`
113	  is outside the vendor set, so a link from any file under `packs/` resolves to nothing in every
114	  consumer — the `reference-integrity` class that reached `main` unnoticed in #424 (and that
115	  check is work-scoped, so it only sees paths the branch itself deletes). Reference `docs/` from
116	  the issue or PR instead.
117	- **A pack's `RULES.md` carries directives an agent must obey — never a walkthrough of how the
118	  feature works** (owner correction, 2026-08-06: *"Rules are context for any agentic work, not for
119	  random explanations"*). The same injection that makes the prose useful makes description
120	  expensive: a paragraph that only *describes* a mechanism is paid for by every session in every
121	  declaring repo and steers none of them. Shipping the fleet-baseline `follow` half, the rule the
122	  change actually added was one sentence — the two extra PAT read scopes a followed run needs —
123	  and everything around it was a feature tour. Behaviour description goes in the module header and
124	  the pack `README.md`, read by whoever works on that code rather than loaded ambiently; the test
125	  before a paragraph goes in is whether an agent could *act* differently for having read it. Same
126	  instinct as the comment rule `basics` now carries (describe the current state, not the change),
127	  applied where the cost is per session rather than per reader.
128	- **Pick a scheduled task's cadence from how often its signal actually moves.** On a member the
129	  mounted canon changes most nights — baselining converges `.claudinite/shared/` daily — so any
130	  precondition reading `sharedMount` fires nearly every night, spending an opus dispatch per
131	  firing. Where the work isn't latency-sensitive (pruning, dedup), a stale item stays harmlessly
132	  correct, so daily buys noise, not freshness: `growth-dedup` moved to `weekly` in #583 and loses
133	  nothing, because the signals are window-scoped (`sinceIso`) and `windowStart` widens to the
134	  widest due task's period — a weekly run sees all 7 days, batched rather than dropped.
135	- **The home doesn't declare `git-github`, so its skills never mount — never conclude "no such
136	  skill" from `.claude/skills/`.** `mount-skills.mjs` filters on the *literal* declaration
137	  (`isActive(p, { packs: declared })`), not the `requires` closure `check_the_world.mjs` resolves,
138	  and the baselining that would normalize that closure into `.claudinite-checks.json` is the one
139	  thing gated `!isHome` — so `merge-to-main` and `git-github-advanced` are simply absent here.
140	  Read `packs/<pack>/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` out of the tracked tree — the corpus *is* this repo,
141	  and an unmounted skill says nothing about whether its procedure applies. The seeding gap above
142	  is a different one (`git-github` arrives by closure, never `seededByDefault`); catching this
143	  one needs `resolveDeclaredPacks` compared against the literal declaration.
144	- **Never re-serialize a repo's JSON config to apply an edit — patch the text.** A round-trip
145	  rewrites what it wasn't asked to: Python's `json.dump` defaults to `ensure_ascii=True` (every
146	  non-ASCII character becomes a `\uXXXX` escape), and indent, key order and the trailing newline
147	  become the serializer's opinion. Nothing fails and tests stay green, so it rides onward. Edit
148	  JSON as anchored text; if you must round-trip, pin every lossy default and read the resulting
149	  diff before committing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `repo-text-sweeps`, where a
150	  `\uXXXX`-in-tracked-JSON check would carry it.)
151	- **Test git fixtures must commit with signing off.** `engine-tests/helpers.mjs`'s `makeRepo`
152	  overrides identity but not signing, so all 31 call sites route fixture commits through the
153	  signing service; when it degrades, each commit blocks on it and the suite leaks descriptors
154	  (~800 per full run against a 4096 cap) until `git commit` and `git push` fail process-wide.
155	  Commit with `git -c commit.gpgsign=false commit --no-gpg-sign`: signing a tmpdir throwaway
156	  buys nothing. (Portable — a promote candidate for `writing-tests`.)
157	- **A canon session with a consumer repo also in its sources will reach for the *consumer's*
158	  merge skill — merge by the skill of the repo you are merging into.** Canon work is routinely
159	  dual-repo (the canon plus the fleet member being piloted), and both repos ship a merge skill
160	  under different names — the canon's `packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/` and, say, GCEC's
161	  local `merge-and-ci`. The consumer's skill wins the match on name/description and is followed
162	  to the letter, so the canon-only steps in *its* recipe are silently skipped — repeatedly, the
163	  **post-merge conversation capture** (`node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue
164	  <n>`, the "After the merge" section of `merge-to-main`). So: before merging in a dual-repo
165	  session, resolve the merge skill **by target repo**, not by which skill matched first — and
166	  treat capture as part of the merge, not as an optional epilogue.
167	- **Fail-soft SessionStart steps hide their own breakage fleet-wide — test the emitted
168	  output, not the exit code.** Every `engine/pack_loader/` SessionStart step
169	  (`inject-pack-prose.mjs`, `mount-skills.mjs`, `env-requirements.mjs`) wraps its body in
170	  `try { ... } catch {}` so a broken loader never blocks a session. That fail-soft is deliberate,
171	  but it means a runtime fault — a wrong dynamic-import target, a renamed module — exits 0 and
172	  simply emits nothing: no error, no signal. And because the engine is vendored verbatim into
173	  every member, one canon regression silently disables that step across the whole fleet at once.
174	  So a step like this must be guarded by a regression test that runs the real script against a
175	  real corpus and asserts the **positive** effect — prose IS emitted — never merely that
176	  `status === 0` (which fail-soft makes meaningless); see
177	  `engine-tests/pack_loader/inject-pack-prose.test.mjs`.
178	- **The nightly self-refresh cannot repair the vendor-set computation — pin operational
179	  files against the REAL canon tree.** Baselining's converge re-runs
180	  `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.mjs` from canon HEAD, so a bug *in that computation* is
181	  the one class of canon regression that is not self-healing: every refresh faithfully
182	  reproduces it, and recovery is an out-of-band vendor refresh applied to each member by
183	  hand. So when the vendor set excludes by *pattern*, an operational file that matches
184	  needs a by-path whitelist (`VENDORED_ENGINE_DOCS`) **and** a regression test asserting
185	  against the real canon tree, not only a synthetic fixture: a fixture keeps proving the
186	  whitelist mechanism works while the live path silently drops out from under it (see the
187	  paired tests in `vendoring/compute-vendor-set.test.mjs`).
188	- **A check that selects its inputs by path pattern can reach zero files and still pass — assert
189	  the live in-scope count.** When skills moved inside their owning pack (#385),
190	  `skill-no-enforcement-narration` kept scanning the root-level `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` layout: it
191	  matched nothing in any tree, read as live, and caught nothing until a human noticed the prose it
192	  should have flagged (#560 — 21 skills in scope once repointed). Its fixtures are why it hid so
193	  well; they spelled the same dead layout, so five green tests proved the *matching* and never the
194	  *selection*. A scan-based check therefore needs one assertion over the **real** tree that its
195	  scope is non-empty. Other half of the same class: agent-facing text pointing where the code isn't
196	  — the same PR fixed a rule whose `why`, fix text and `doc` all named `engine/checks_helpers` or
197	  `checks/lib`, neither of which ever existed. Nothing catches that on its own —
198	  `reference-integrity` is work-scoped and flags only paths the branch itself deletes — so grep the
199	  tree for any directory you name in a finding, a remedy, or a doc pointer before shipping it.
200	- **A scheduled task's precondition gates on movement in the window, never on standing state.** "An
201	  open PR exists" is true forever once it is true once, so the task wakes every night, spends an
202	  agent, and re-derives yesterday's verdict over an unchanged set (three of tidy-repo's tasks
203	  shipped that way; fixed in #554). Gate on the objects' own movement — a `touched` list or a
204	  tip-commit date, which the signal collector has to actually carry (`branches` carried names only,
205	  so "is any of this new" had no answer at all). A signal that is true most days on an active repo
206	  — a substantive `main` move — may only **widen** an already-triggered run, never wake one. And the
207	  gate is not the scope: where a verdict is relative to the rest of the set (superseded-by,
208	  already-in-`main`), newness gates and the full set stays the scope. (Portable — a promote
209	  candidate for `basics/scheduled-tasks.md`, which states the precondition contract but not this.)
210	- **You cannot force a due slot by running the scheduler workflow by hand.** Dueness is
211	  stateless — a slot is due iff its time falls in `(last successful run, now]` — so a
212	  `workflow_dispatch` run outside the slot's window succeeds, prints `- no tasks due`, and
213	  does nothing. It looks like a healthy run. To exercise a task Action-side, invoke its
214	  worker directly, or move the slot hour in `taskScheduler` and wait for the cron.
215	- **A scheduled task is gated twice — prove a change through `planRun`, never through its own
216	  precondition.** `planRun` computes the due list *before* any precondition runs, so a task whose
217	  most-recent slot has already been run is never evaluated and never reads its signals at all. #513's
218	  forced-run override landed with every test driving the precondition (or the signal collector) directly
219	  and was inert on exactly the run it existed for — the mid-day manual trigger — because the due-list
220	  gate it never touched had already dropped the task (`evaluations: []`; fixed in #516). A test that
221	  starts *inside* the gate proves only "works once evaluated" and says nothing about whether the task
222	  ever gets there. Drive the real `planRun` from a deliberately **non-due** slot: that is the only shape
223	  that catches it.
224	- **Every due task in a run shares ONE checkout — an agentless worker must not touch it.** The
225	  scheduler runs the whole due list in a single working tree, so a worker that checks out a branch or
226	  leaves an index behind hands the next task a tree it did not expect, and a run that dies leaves the
227	  mess for whatever follows. A task whose output is a regenerated file lands it through
228	  `engine/scheduler/deliver-generated.mjs` — git plumbing against the fetched base tip, with HEAD, the
229	  index and the working tree untouched — and reads its prior state from that base rather than local
230	  HEAD, so stacked runs stay idempotent. (`basics/baselining`'s own deliver is the deliberate
231	  exception: it commits a whole working tree and re-cuts a dated family branch; the landing itself —
232	  delivery preference, CI dispatch, arm/land/merge — is shared, in `engine/scheduler/land-pr.mjs`.)
233	- **A code-search hit is evidence; a code-search miss is not — survey by reading each file.**
234	- **Derive the test file list from the tree — every hand-written glob here under-runs the suite.**
235	  There is no `package.json` and no test script, so each session invents its own incantation and
236	  silently verifies less than it thinks. Measured in this checkout: `node --test <dir>` does not
237	  recurse — it resolves the path as a module and dies with `Cannot find module`; bash `**` is not
238	  recursive without `globstar`, so `engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs` reaches
239	  **37 of 65** tracked test files. Four consecutive sessions (2026-07-26, #459/#452/#435/#468) each
240	  wrote a different command and reported 587, 690, 621 and 697 tests — three of them pushed after
241	  running a strict subset. Neither published list is authoritative either: `ci.yml`'s `tests=(…)`
242	  array omits `vendoring/*.test.mjs`, and `engine/checks/README.md`'s "as CI runs it" one-liner
243	  names `engine/test/`, `skills/` and `mount/`, none of which exist. So enumerate from git and let
244	  the count speak: `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. (The drift-guard, once the array is
245	  clean: assert every tracked `*.test.mjs` is matched by `ci.yml`'s globs.)
246	- **A branch that waited overnight has lost its base *and* possibly its premise — re-verify the
247	  problem still exists on current `main`, unasked.** This repo merges its own scheduled-task PRs
248	  without a human, on top of multi-phase migrations that retire whole directories: measured on
249	  PR #465, `main` moved **14 commits in 13.7 hours** and one of them (#473, "retire `run_daily/`")
250	  *deleted the file the PR's diagnosis rested on* and had already landed most of its content. The
251	  branch rebased cleanly and the tests stayed green — the change was simply no longer the change to
252	  make, and the correct move was `git checkout -B <branch> origin/main` and re-applying only the
253	  surviving slice (9 files → 2). So syncing the base is not the check; the check is a **content**
254	  one: after `git fetch`, read what the new commits did to the surface you are changing and state
255	  whether the problem is still there, what the goal was, and what survives. Do this whenever you
