1	# Working discipline
2	
3	The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.
4	
5	Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.
6	
7	Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
8	
9	1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
10	2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
11	3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
12	
13	The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.
14	
15	Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.
16	
17	**Minimize every task's shelf-life — the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.** An open task is a standing tax: whoever returns to it pays a full reload of the context that was free while the work was hot. So finish a change by **watching it work now** — never park it on "check tomorrow", which is almost always the wrong choice in any context. A change to scheduled or unattended machinery does not wait for its next natural run — force one now (the scheduler's `FORCE_TASKS` lever, a `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state; those levers exist precisely so verification can happen while the change is still in someone's head. The same yardstick governs **migration planning**: prefer the design that converges in one forced pass over the one that trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must remember to close. When verifying now is genuinely impossible (an external release window, an upstream fix in flight), the follow-up must be a mechanism that comes to you — a scheduled task, a watched PR, an issue something converges — never a human's memory.
18	
19	When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.
20	
21	When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."
22	
23	Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.
24	
25	Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.
26	
27	Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.
28	
29	When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.
30	
31	An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.
32	
33	# The task lifecycle
34	
35	The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.
36	
37	For every new task:
38	
39	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
40	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
41	3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
42	
43	# Engineering practices
44	
45	General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project — portable, shared rules; project-specific rules (architecture, test mechanics) live in the consuming repo's own docs. The portable git/GitHub-operational practices — branch/commit history, merging, automated-job branches — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md); the mechanics of searching and rewriting text across files — grep/sed sweeps, renames, broken references — live in [the repo-text-sweeps skill](skills/repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md); the practices for writing trustworthy tests — see-it-fail, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, coverage gating — live in [the writing-tests skill](skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md); and how to investigate a bug and pin down its root cause — version-gap triage, re-deriving after a failed fix, probing for a real datapoint — lives in [the bug-investigation skill](skills/bug-investigation/SKILL.md).
46	
47	- Name by scope/responsibility, not technology or mechanism.
48	- Keep a single source of truth for derived or duplicated data — generate the rest from it instead of hand-editing, and have a test fail if it drifts. Split a fact across more than one place only when a technological constraint forbids a single home, and then have the drift-guard test state, in its own text, the two-or-more places it watches and why the split is forced — so an invisible coupling becomes a self-documenting, reviewed one, and the next reader knows the duplication is deliberate and where its other half lives. When the duplicate mirrors executable logic you can't generate from (e.g. a static list shadowing a set of predicate/matcher functions), drift-guard it by *executing the real logic* against the list in both directions — every entry accepted by some predicate, and every predicate satisfied by some entry — rather than parsing the logic out. When a value must be copied into files that can't share an import (a label spanning a YAML workflow guard and a JS module; a repo slug in prod code and its test), declare it as a `sharedConstants` entry in `.claudinite-checks.json` — its `value`, the expected per-file `counts`, and a `what` naming the places and why. Declared counts are matched against the *flat* literal (comments included), so keep a guarded value on one line wherever it appears — an occurrence wrapped across a line break is invisible to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. For a value that must stay in sync but *changes over time* (a version string bumped each release), set `regex: true` and give a pattern instead of a literal — every match must then be identical across the declared files, so the guard never needs re-pinning on a bump.
49	- Honor separation of concerns in what you write — code comments and Markdown instructions alike: when file A uses or references file B (a module A imports, or a doc/procedure set A points to), A may state *what* it needs from B or *that* it delegates to B, but never restate *how* B does its job or re-spell the procedures B owns. B's mechanism lives in one place — with B. Copying it into A leaks B's internals across the boundary and springs the same drift trap as any duplicated source of truth: change B and A's paraphrase silently goes stale, with nothing to catch it. Point to B instead of paraphrasing it.
50	- One commit per concern: two changes that could each stand alone — separately revertible, cherry-pickable, bisectable — don't share a commit, and a message that numbers unrelated items is describing the split it should have been. More commits is not the goal: once a commit is in, later work is a *new* commit, never a rewrite of the one that landed.
51	- Name any file a test autogenerates with `GENERATED` in its filename (e.g. `foo.GENERATED.md`, `foo.baseline.GENERATED.json`) so it's unmistakable at a glance. Don't hand-edit a GENERATED file, and never resolve its merge conflict by hand: take either side to clear the markers, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit its output. Hand-editing desyncs it from its source — and when the other branch changed the generator's logic, only a re-run produces correct values. Automate the "take either side" step itself where you can: assign the file a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry (plus a one-time `git config merge.ours.driver true` per clone) so a conflicting merge on it resolves automatically instead of needing the markers cleared by hand first; `git config rerere.enabled true` similarly replays a manual conflict resolution automatically the next time the same conflict recurs.
52	- Verify how a platform or runtime actually behaves against authoritative docs or a real run — not against a comment or a prior commit's claim.
53	- Prove a *behaviour-preserving* optimisation actually preserves behaviour before trusting it — "it should be equivalent" is not evidence. Fingerprint the full outputs (hash them) and exercise the old and new paths across *every* branch (fuzz the inputs that select each), accepting the change only on a bit-identical match. And it is legitimate to leave a hot path un-optimised when the correctness risk of rewriting it outweighs the speed-up — record that as a deliberate call, not an oversight.
54	- Earn each dependency: prefer a built-in (or a few lines) for a narrow job, and drop one when the assumption that justified it lapses.
55	- Before adding production code for a raised edge case (a review's "what about scenario X?"), check whether the system's existing composed rules already produce the right answer — behaviour that emerges from a composition of independent rules (a pure reducer, a set of matchers) is often already covered, sometimes on more than one independent count. When it is, add no production code: pin it with a regression test — and an accept criterion under the relevant requirement, where you track those — asserting the contrast case too, so the test would bite if the rule interaction ever changed.
56	- A bespoke how-to earns its place only by what it adds over authoritative external docs — our own failure modes, gotchas, and the exact path we ran. Before writing one, check it against those docs and keep only the additive parts; a guide that re-explains upstream (often less well) is worse than a link to upstream plus a short gotchas list. And document/recommend only a path you've actually run, not the "standard" or seemingly-better one you haven't.
57	- Resilience that swallows errors destroys observability — during development, before a solution is proven right, add debugging information first, and remove it later.
58	- A capability applied **best-effort behind a silent fallback** (a probe-gated optimisation, an optional hardware/platform feature, a hint the runtime may ignore) must **record whether it actually engaged** — read the state back where the platform exposes it, and log which path ran. Without that, every later measurement of the feature is uninterpretable: a session where it quietly never engaged looks exactly like one where it did and didn't help, so the data says nothing about the feature and a bug report about it can't be diagnosed. The fallback keeps the run alive; the record is what keeps it *evaluable*.
59	- Keep everything the software persists on a user's machine under **one** user-deletable location. "Delete that folder and it's gone" is a promise users act on — someone who deletes it believes the whole record went with it — so a new storage need extends that location rather than earning a second one, and anything the platform forces outside it (a registration the OS owns) is named explicitly as the exception.
60	- A user-facing statement about what the software does with a user's data — a permission prompt's usage string, a privacy policy, a store-listing disclosure — is part of the behaviour's contract, not documentation of it. Change the behaviour and the statement changes **in the same commit**; a stale disclosure is worse than a blunt one. And read the direction the other way too: retaining something previously not retained, adding an outbound connection, or opening a listener is a change to the *promise*, not a new field — it earns an explicit decision, and the disclosure rewrite, before the code.
61	- When a session will drive an external runtime more than once (a headless browser, a device, a REPL, a deploy target), write **one** parameterised driver script into the scratchpad and re-point it — take the target, the selector, and the output path from argv — rather than authoring a fresh throwaway per invocation. A re-run costs seconds; re-authoring costs 15–20 s each and re-derives the same setup every time, which is where a surprising share of a long session's wall clock goes.
62	- When automating a task that requires live AI conversation context (e.g., a reflection pass over a session), hook it to an existing human workflow event rather than background infrastructure — shell hooks lack conversation access and fire at per-turn granularity, not session-end. The cheapest trigger is often a change to an existing command's definition.
63	- In a pipeline or CI workflow, treat expected, handled outcomes (known-bad inputs, anticipated stops) as clean exits with a comment — not failures. Reserve the failure signal for genuine breakage; a red run should always be a surprise.
64	- A live fetch that works on your machine can fail from CI or a sandbox (403/400, a CAPTCHA wall) because the *datacenter IP* is blocked, not the User-Agent — browser-like headers won't change that. Route the fetch through a residential-proxy service (these usually render JS too, so a single-page app records real content) rather than tweaking headers; treat targets that stay blocked even through a proxy as un-cacheable.
65	- `pkill -f "<pattern>"` matches the *invoking shell's own* command line too, so a pattern naming the process you want also names the shell that typed it — the shell dies, and everything chained after the `pkill` (`;`, `&&`) is silently dropped, with the run reporting only a bare non-zero exit. Never chain a `-f` pkill; and break the self-match by bracketing one character of the pattern (`pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`), which still matches the target but no longer matches the literal you just typed.
66	- A cloud/root setup script may start in the repo's *parent* directory, not the checkout — a bare `npm ci` / build there finds no manifest and silently does nothing, surfacing much later as a confusing missing-deps error. Make the setup script `cd` into the checkout before running anything.
67	- A `Cannot find module …` (or other missing-dependency) error on a *fresh* checkout almost always means the install hasn't run there yet, not a code bug — `node_modules` and other vendored dependency dirs start empty on a clone and on an ephemeral CI/sandbox checkout. Run the install and re-run before hunting for a code-level cause.
68	- Collapse a property tracked in more than one place (a spec tag, a side manifest, a per-item field) into a single source of truth, preferring a *structural* classifier — one derived from where the item lives (its folder or path) — over a hand-set field: a structural classifier has no field to forget to update and can't desync from the item it classifies.
69	- Avoid a default value; require it explicitly, or make it structural (derived from where the thing lives). A default moves the real value into a fallback (`x || DEFAULT`) plus a comment documenting it — two things that drift, neither visible at the call site — all to save a little typing. When automation maintains many instances of a config (a fleet of repos, generated project files), have the automation **materialize the explicit value into every file it maintains** instead of interpreting absence: the knob then sits visibly in the exact file where anyone would go to change it, and a missing key becomes drift the automation repairs rather than a case code must interpret (e.g. the fleet baselining writing `"maintenance": { "delivery": "auto" }` into each member's `.claudinite-checks.json`).
70	- When a check that walks a file tree (an orphan/reachability scan, a doc audit, a lint) must ignore files you don't own — a synced submodule, a vendored dependency, generated output — derive its file set from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with a hardcoded path-to-skip. There's no exclude path to maintain, it can't desync when an artifact moves, and it stays correct when a new gitignored directory appears. Git already knows what you own; tracked vs. ignored is the exact distinction. The price of that precision: a *brand-new* file is untracked, so it sits outside the sweep until it is committed — the run's own "checked N files" line is **not** evidence your new file was among them. Commit (or `git add`) first, then re-run, before reading a green sweep as coverage of what you just wrote.
71	- A check that scans source for a forbidden token (a banned API, an impure import, a DOM specific) must match *code, not prose* — strip comments before you match, or a comment that merely names the token (`// saved in chrome.storage`) fails the build over an English sentence, and the next author who documents the very rule you're enforcing trips it. Strip *string-aware*: a `//` inside `"https://…"` is not a comment, and blindly deleting to end-of-line corrupts real code (and can hide a genuine violation later on that line). The corpus's reusable helper is `stripComments` in [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); a project whose scan can't import it (e.g. a test that runs where the mount is absent) should inline the same string-aware pass and point a comment back at that canonical source.
72	- A comment describes the code's *current state*, never the edit that produced it. Don't explain the change you just made, and don't explain an absence — a comment saying something was removed, renamed, or "no longer" done describes a version of the file the reader can't see and doesn't need; the diff and the commit message are where change history belongs, and they keep it accurate without maintenance. State the reason the code is the way it is now, or write nothing. The same applies to a comment that narrates a fix in the past tense ("switched to X because Y broke"): keep only the part still true of the code in front of you ("X, because Y can't handle Z"), and drop the rest.
73	- Comments are not free: each one is a claim the next reader must verify against the code, and a claim that will drift. Add one only when it carries something the code cannot — more comments help only when each pays for itself, and a comment that restates the code costs attention while adding nothing.
74	- A comment should carry the *why* or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself — not a fact already reconstructable from same-file code plus a known convention (a restated fact drifts out of sync as the code changes, silently). When a comment must name another file, state its exact path in exactly one canonical place and have every other mention point at that reference or the concept, not re-spell the path — a path repeated across many comments turns every future move into comment-churn the code itself never needed.

# The CANON repo's own CI — Claudinite's test suite + its own conformance sweep
# on every PR. Not consumer wiring (consumers ship no workflow, #385).
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  # Dispatchable so a GITHUB_TOKEN-authored PR (whose push/open GitHub never
  # turns into a pull_request run — the recursion guard) can still get this
  # suite started on its branch: baselining's deliver() and any bot flow like
  # migrations-retire's archive PR (#432, #565) dispatch it explicitly.
  workflow_dispatch:
defaults:
  run:
    shell: bash
jobs:
  test-and-conformance:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          # Check out the PR's real head, not the synthetic refs/pull/N/merge commit
          # actions/checkout uses by default — otherwise HEAD is an ephemeral merge of
          # the branch into main, which the work-scoped squash-merge-history check would
          # (correctly, for that synthetic commit) flag. This makes CI evaluate exactly
          # what the local Stop hook does: the branch tip. Falls back to github.sha on push.
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.sha }}
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - name: Unit tests
        # THE test roots — a closed set of FOLDERS, each swept to any depth. Depth is
        # deliberately not enumerated: the previous form spelled out one glob per level
        # (`packs-tests/*/skills/*/*.test.mjs` and so on), so a test at an unlisted depth
        # was silently never run — which is exactly how vendoring/'s two files sat outside
        # CI. `**` removes depth from the question; what remains is the root list, and
        # engine-tests/ci-test-roots.test.mjs fails the moment a tracked test lands
        # outside it. Adding a root is a deliberate CI edit; adding a test is not.
        #   engine-tests/            engine/ + the other top-level canon code (migrations/, …);
        #                            mirrors engine/'s inner structure, and stays canon-side
        #                            because engine/ ships to consumers exactly as-is (#385)
        #   packs-tests/             every canon pack's tests, mirroring packs/
        #   vendoring/               co-located with the vendor computer/writer they cover
        #   dev/tools/               maintainer-side tooling nothing at session time runs
        #   .claudinite/local/packs/ this repo's own local packs — tests live inside the tree
        # nullglob: a root with no tests drops out instead of reaching node as a literal pattern.
        run: |
          shopt -s globstar nullglob
          tests=(engine-tests/**/*.test.mjs packs-tests/**/*.test.mjs vendoring/**/*.test.mjs dev/tools/**/*.test.mjs .claudinite/local/packs/**/*.test.mjs)
          node --test "${tests[@]}"
      - name: Conformance sweep
        # The world sweep's home is the test/CI flow (not the Stop hook, which
        # carries only the work scope) — this canon repo models the pattern
        # bootstrap wires into consumers. World only: the work scope judges a
        # session's change and runs at that session's Stop hook, not here.
        run: node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs
      - name: Promote write-surface gate
        # The growth promote stage (.claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/tasks/growth-promote/task.md)
        # is the one change bounded to packs/ + skills/ — an ordinary engine PR legitimately edits
        # checks/ and engine/, so this cannot run on every PR. It keys on the promote branch prefix
        # (the task doc pins it) and fails the promote PR if a changed path strays.
        if: contains(github.head_ref, 'growth-promote')
        run: node .claudinite/local/packs/canon-curation/promote-scope.mjs

1	# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy
2	
3	The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
4	pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
5	the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
6	([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
7	[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
8	[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).
9	
10	The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**
11	
12	- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
13	  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
14	  ref's auto-generated name.
15	- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
16	  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
17	  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
18	  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.
19	
20	Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
21	**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
22	rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
23	three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

1	# sheepdog — the fleet enforcer marker
2	
3	Declaring this pack marks a repo as the **fleet enforcer**: the one repo that covers and maintains
4	every repo under an owner. It's opt-in — a dedicated `sheepdog` repo declares it (it is **not** seeded
5	by `--init`).
6	
7	It contributes the pieces only a fleet enforcer needs — four **cross-repo sweeps** — plus their config
8	schema and the scheduled tasks that run them. The rest of the machinery — running the daily-run (the
9	orchestrator), the task engine (`engine/scheduler/`), scheduling — is Claudinite **core**, because
10	baselining and the daily-run are Claudinite's own responsibility, not the pack's.
11	
12	**Four sweeps, four questions** — separate, because they close on unrelated conditions. The
13	**census** ([check-fleet-coverage.mjs](tasks/fleet-census/check-fleet-coverage.mjs)) asks *is this repo a
14	member* and converges `fleet-adoption` issues. The **freshness sweep**
15	([check-fleet-freshness.mjs](tasks/fleet-freshness/check-fleet-freshness.mjs)) takes coverage as given, asks *is that
16	membership still meaning anything*, and converges `fleet-drift` issues. The second exists because
17	per-project scheduling made every member maintain itself and removed the last outside look at one:
18	self-maintenance cannot detect its own absence. The **usage sweep**
19	([aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs](tasks/fleet-usage/aggregate-fleet-usage.mjs)) asks *what does the fleet
20	actually use* and writes `usage-fleet.GENERATED.json` — a file, not issues, because it reports a
21	measurement rather than a condition to converge. It exists because a member folds its own skill-usage
22	numbers and can therefore only say whether a skill loads *there*; whether a skill earns its place at
23	all is fleet-shaped, and nothing inside a member can see it. The **pack-seed sweep**
24	([check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs](tasks/fleet-pack-seeds/check-fleet-pack-seeds.mjs)) asks *does each member
25	declare what this fleet standardizes on* and **adds the declaration** where it is missing. It exists
26	because some packs need a parameter no member can derive — the answer is a fact about the fleet, and canon
27	cannot supply it either, since a bootstrap run does not know which fleet it is bootstrapping into. Only
28	this repo knows: it is the fleet.
29	
30	**The pack-seed sweep is the one that writes to members**, and it stays narrow on purpose: one pack
31	declaration from this repo's `packSeeds` list, one PUT to the member's default branch guarded by the blob
32	sha the read returned, idempotent, no issue in either direction. Three rules keep it safe. It **names no
33	pack** — every id comes from the config, so the enforcer never becomes a second place packs are known. It
34	**gates on the member's own mount**: a declared pack whose code is absent is a blocking `config` error
35	there, and a member's mount carries only what it declared as of its last converge, so the sweep writes
36	only where the pack is already on disk — `not-vendored` is a wait, not a finding, and members converge
37	nightly, so the rollout needs no coordination. And it **seeds, never overrides**: a member that already
38	declares the pack, or already carries a config for it, keeps both — the fleet's list is a floor, and a
39	choice a repo made is a decision the sweep cannot second-guess. A dormant member is never written to.
40	
41	A pack arriving with canon reaches the fleet that already exists through a **baseline migration** instead
42	(a `declarePacks` op, applied by each member's own baselining in the same transactional commit that
43	vendors the pack's code). This sweep is the **standing** half: a migration record is dated and retires,
44	while the sweep keeps converging every member the fleet acquires after it is gone.
45	
46	**One manual lever, not a fifth sweep** — [force-fleet-baseline.mjs](fleet-baseline/force-fleet-baseline.mjs)
47	fires every covered member's own `claudinite-scheduler.yml` with `overrides: FORCE_TASKS=baselining`,
48	which is the same button the owner would press in that repo's Actions tab, pressed across the fleet in
49	one run. It is a **dispatcher, not a maintainer**: each member converges its own mount, with its own
50	token, under its own delivery policy, and this writes nothing to any member — one queued Actions run
51	each, and no commit, issue or comment. Under per-project scheduling the fleet needs no push in the
52	ordinary case; this is for the un-ordinary ones — a canon change the fleet should pick up *now*, or the
53	tail of members whose next slot is hours away while someone is standing by. A forced run bypasses
54	baselining's precondition, so a member with nothing to do converges to a cheap no-op: over-using it is
55	wasteful, never unsafe. A **dormant** member is skipped and reported (it stopped its own scheduler on
56	purpose); `include_dormant` overrides that. Canon is skipped — its baselining self-skips — but the
57	enforcer repo is **not**: it is an ordinary member, and leaving it out would make the one repo the owner
58	is watching the one repo that did not move.
59	
60	**Why that one is a workflow** — every other thing this pack does answers a recurring question, so it
61	is a scheduled task. Force-baseline answers none and has no cadence: it is owner-initiated, carries its
62	own inputs (repo filter, dry run, dormant opt-in, follow), and starts when a human presses *Run workflow*. Its
63	workflow declares **`workflow_dispatch` only** — no `schedule:` — so the vendored scheduler remains the
64	repo's only cron and [scheduled-tasks.md](../basics/scheduled-tasks.md)'s doctrine is untouched. GitHub
65	reads workflows solely from a repo's own `.github/`, never from the mount, so the enforcer hosts a copy
66	of [stubs/workflows/fleet-baseline.yml](stubs/workflows/fleet-baseline.yml) — byte-identical, carrying
67	no repo-specific value.
68	
69	**It arrives, and stays current, on its own** — through the
70	[`sheepdog-fleet-baseline`](../../migrations/active_migrations/2026-08-05-sheepdog-fleet-baseline.mjs)
71	record, gated on the repo **declaring this pack**, so declaring sheepdog is the whole adoption. Its
72	delivery takes one detour worth knowing about: the Action's `GITHUB_TOKEN` may not write under
73	`.github/workflows/`, so the nightly converge **withholds** the file from its own push and baselining's
74	**agent stage** lands it on the same maintenance branch over MCP, whose credential does hold that
75	permission ([#649](https://github.com/[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]/issues/649); the mechanism is
76	`withheldWorkflowPaths` in the baselining worker and §2b of its task.md). Nothing about that is
77	sheepdog-specific — the scheduler workflow itself rides the same path — and nothing about it needs a
78	human. Edit the pack; the copy follows.
79	
80	**Where the code lives** — each sweep sits **inside its task's folder**, because only that task's
81	`worker.mjs` uses it; force-baseline sits in [fleet-baseline/](fleet-baseline/) beside them, because it
82	belongs to no task and its runner is the vendored workflow. The pack root holds just what they all
83	need: [fleet-api.mjs](fleet-api.mjs) (cross-repo REST primitives — read-only toward members but for the
84	one `putFile` the pack-seed sweep needs) and
85	[fleet-config.mjs](fleet-config.mjs) (the one reader of the entry `config` below).
86	
87	**Config** — this repo's `.claudinite-checks.json` carries, as its `packs` entry for this pack:
88	
89	```json
90	{ "id": "sheepdog", "config": { "owner": "missingbulb", "kind": "user", "exclude": ["owner/repo-a"],
91	                                "canonRepo": "[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]", "staleDays": 14,
92	                                "packSeeds": [{ "id": "<a pack>", "config": { … } }] } }
93	```
94	
95	`owner` (default: this repo's owner) is who to cover; `exclude` is the repos deliberately kept out of
96	the fleet (a full `owner/name` each) — a repo is kept out by adding it here. `kind: "user"` today; org
97	support is a later addition. `canonRepo` (default `<owner>/Claudinite`) is what a member's stamped ref
98	is measured against — named rather than inferred, because a ref tells you nothing about where it came
99	from. `staleDays` (default `14`) is how far behind is too far. `packSeeds` (default: **none**) is what
100	this fleet wants every member to declare — each `{ id, config? }`, seeded into members that lack it. This
101	list is the **only** place a pack is named: the sweep carries the mechanism, the fleet carries the
102	choice. All three default, so an existing sheepdog config keeps working untouched.
103	
104	**Classification** — all four sweeps are ordinary **pack tasks**, not fleet mechanisms. Their
105	*implementation* — an account-spanning PAT — happens to scan every repo under the owner, but their
106	declaration, scheduling, and lifecycle are exactly those of any pack task. None declares the
107	`fleet` signal nor `session_scope: fleet`; the cross-repo reach lives in the implementation, never in
108	how a task is wired. (The task files carry the same note.)
109	
110	**How they run** — as the pack's [`fleet-census`](tasks/fleet-census/task.md) (`daily`),
111	[`fleet-freshness`](tasks/fleet-freshness/task.md) (`weekly`),
112	[`fleet-usage`](tasks/fleet-usage/task.md) (`daily`) and
113	[`fleet-pack-seeds`](tasks/fleet-pack-seeds/task.md) (`daily`) scheduled tasks, all `agent_model: none`,
114	each with its sweep as `prework`. All are `expected_outcome: none` except usage
115	(`merged-pr`), because its output IS a tracked file and an
116	auto-merging PR keeps that write inside the outcome taxonomy, lets this repo's CI gate a malformed
117	file, and makes the daily PR stream a browsable audit trail. The pack-seed sweep is `none` for a
118	different reason: its write goes to **other** repos, and the ceiling describes what a task may do to its
119	own. Freshness is weekly because drift is
120	measured in days — a daily sweep would re-ask a question whose answer cannot have changed; usage is
121	daily because the members fold daily; pack seeds is daily because a member becomes writable the moment
122	its nightly converge vendors the pack, and daily makes that "the next morning". There is **no coverage workflow** — preprocessing
123	runs Action-side inside this repo's one scheduler workflow, so the repo Actions secret is already
124	reachable there; each task's `required_secrets: ['FLEET_GITHUB_TOKEN']` stamps the name into that
125	workflow's env and is what asks the owner for it (a fine-grained PAT spanning the owner's repos:
126	Metadata read, **Contents read and write**, Issues read/write — freshness adds no scope, and the
127	pack-seed sweep is what raises Contents from read-only across the fleet to read/write, because writing
128	one declaration into each member is its whole job; Contents write on this repo also covers
129	baseline-migration retirement). A workflow that exists only to hold a secret is redundant
130	([packs/basics/scheduled-tasks.md](../basics/scheduled-tasks.md)) — the force-baseline workflow above is
131	not that: it exists because the operation is manual, and it reads the same secret only incidentally.
132	
133	**The one scope the sweeps don't need** — force-baseline adds **Actions: read and write** on the owner's
134	repositories to that PAT. Dispatching another repo's workflow is an Actions *write*, so a token scoped
135	for the sweeps alone answers `403` on every member. The sweep reports that per repo as
136	`no-permission` and fails the run rather than retrying: it is a grant to fix once, not a transient. The
137	sweeps themselves are unaffected — they never dispatch anything. Watching what it dispatched adds two
138	more *read* scopes to the same PAT — **Pull requests: read** and **Issues: read**; without them a
139	followed run reports every member as unfinished, and never the reverse.
140	
141	**What freshness assumes** — baselining reverts a stamp-only bump, so `claudinite.updated` advances
142	only when canon changed that member's vendor set. Age of the **stamped ref** is therefore the honest
143	liveness measure, and `behind` reads *"has not picked canon up in `staleDays`"*, not *"canon moved"*.
144	A member whose vendor set genuinely saw no change in the window is the one false positive; `staleDays`
145	is the knob, and the drift issue says so.
146	
147	**Full-roster reporting** — every sweep's report enumerates the whole fleet, not just its findings.
148	Each repo under the owner lands in the report under exactly one named state — covered, dormant,
149	uncovered, opted out, archived/fork, unknown, fresh, behind, out of scope, inactive today, skipped
150	with a reason — and the repos a sweep deliberately never measures (the enforcer itself, canon) are
151	named as such rather than silently absent. The sheepdog provides data on the fleet regardless of
152	state: a roster that names only the exceptions has silent holes, and a reader cannot tell "fine"
153	from "fell out of the report".
154	
155	**When they fail** — a repo the census cannot classify is `unknown`, never uncovered; a member the
156	freshness sweep cannot probe is `unknown`, never behind; a member the pack-seed sweep cannot read or
157	write is `unknown`, never assumed converged: no issue opened, no open issue closed on its
158	behalf, and a non-zero exit. A non-zero preprocessing subprocess fails the task, and the scheduler
159	converges one open `needs-human` issue for it.

1	# canon-curation
2	
3	Claudinite's own curation duties — the fleet-facing work only **Claudinite** runs: promoting
4	members' lessons into the shared canon, sweeping the fleet's stacks for technologies the canon does
5	not yet home, and policing the corpus's `packs/` tree. (The
6	prose-to-checks backlog sweep is no longer canon-only — it moved to
7	[grow_with_claudinite](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) as a per-repo task with a
8	`pack_paths` config, so every repo sweeps its own packs and Claudinite also its core `packs/`.) A
9	**local pack** of the canon home
10	(`.claudinite/local/packs/`, by owner decision 2026-07-19: Claudinite-maintaining-Claudinite is
11	project-specific content, so it lives on the home's own capture surface, not in the portable
12	canon): `detect: null`, never seeded by `--init` or any migration, declared by hand in exactly one
13	repo — the canon home itself, as `local/canon-curation`. Its `tasks/<name>/` folders are found by
14	the home repo's own scheduler exactly like a canon pack's.
15	
16	**Declaration cardinality is the mechanism.** A pack's tasks run once per *declaring* repo, so a
17	pack only the home repo declares yields exactly one dispatch per task per slot — "central, once"
18	with no bespoke orchestrator step. Un-declaring the pack freezes canon absorption without touching
19	the members' side ([grow_with_claudinite](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md)).
20	
21	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| `growth-promote` | a participating member changed its local packs in the window | a PR against Claudinite's `main` |
24	| `growth-discover-packs` | weekly, over every covered member | a PR against Claudinite's `main` |
25	| `migrations-retire` | a fully-applied migration record has passed its TTL | a PR against Claudinite's `main` |
26	
27	| Rule (≤5 words) | How enforced |
28	|---|---|
29	| Pack prose: no enforcement narration | check `pack-no-enforcement-narration` |
30	| Packs import only own + engine | contributed barrier `pack-independence` ([pack-independence.mjs](pack-independence.mjs) — pure data; the [barriers pack](../../../../packs/barriers/README.md) builds the rule) |
31	
32	- **[tasks/growth-promote/](tasks/growth-promote/task.md)** — the growth lifecycle's central stage: read the changed members'
33	  local packs, **generalize** the portable lessons, route each to the right canon home, and open a
34	  PR for the owner to approve. When a portable lesson's technology has no pack home, it mints a
35	  fingerprinted **stub pack** (in its own dedicated PR). This is the sole judgment gate before
36	  shared canon.
37	- **[tasks/growth-discover-packs/](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)** — the weekly **fleet sweep** for
38	  technologies the canon does not yet home: read every member's stack, fold the members into one view
39	  (so first-sight dedup is free — the third member using a technology is the same gap as the first),
40	  and open an owner-reviewed PR authoring the missing `packs/<tech>/`. Its per-repo namesake in
41	  [grow_with_claudinite](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)
42	  is the other side of that line — it authors a repo's own **local** packs and may never re-create what
43	  a canon pack homes, so only this task can close a canon gap. (Promote's stub-minting is narrower
44	  still: one lesson's technology, minted as a seed; this task authors from the whole fleet's usage.)
45	- **[item-routing.md](item-routing.md)** — the shared worthiness + routing method promote (and an
46	  owner-requested retrospective pass) defers to, so every decision about admitting and placing an
47	  item is made the same way.
48	- **[promote-scope.mjs](promote-scope.mjs)** — the CI write-surface gate on promote's PRs: promote
49	  may write only under `packs/` and `skills/` (keyed on the `growth-promote` branch prefix).
50	
51	## The growth lifecycle — three independent stages, no barriers
52	
53	How a lesson is learned in a consuming project, lifted into the shared canon when it's portable,
54	and pruned back out of the project once the canon owns it. Two packs split it by who declares them:
55	**[grow_with_claudinite](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md)** (member-side: extract + dedup + pack
56	discovery, seeded, opt-out by removal) and **canon-curation** (this pack, the central stage).
57	
58	```
59	EXTRACT   per member    → auto-merging PR against the member's main   (grow_with_claudinite)
60	PROMOTE   central, once → PR against Claudinite's main                (canon-curation)
61	DEDUP     per member    → PR against the member's main                (grow_with_claudinite)
62	```
63	
64	All three are ordinary, **independent** planner units — there is no barrier and no phase ordering.
65	Each stage reads only what is already **merged**: promote processes whatever sits on members' mains
66	when it runs, so a lesson extracted tonight is promoted **tomorrow** night (the extract PR's merge
67	shows up in the next night's local-pack signal), and reaches other members' dedup once the promote PR
68	is approved and merged. That approval was always the dominant latency, so the barrier machinery bought little;
69	if the cadence ever matters, promote can run more often (twice daily, or before and after the
70	nightly) without any design change.
71	
72	**Review gates by blast radius, not uniformly.** Promote opens a PR — it's the sole judgment gate
73	before the shared canon every repo reads, so it always needs a human eye. Dedup opens a PR too — a
74	wrongful prune deletes a real local lesson. Extract lands through an **auto-merging PR** against the
75	member's `main` — it writes only that project's own local packs, so it earns a CI gate and a PR trail
76	but not a human reviewer; auto-merge keeps the fleet's daily lesson-capture from flooding review
77	requests. (An owner-requested, in-session retrospective delivers a PR for a human to review — see
78	[extracting-lessons.md](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/extracting-lessons.md).)
79	
80	**Central execution, no plumbing.** Promote runs from the Claudinite home repo with a fleet-wide
81	token, so it reads every participating member and opens its canon PR directly here — no
82	consumer-side Action, no cross-repo PAT, no labelled-issue up-path. The planner hands its gate the
83	`fleetMembers` aggregate (which members changed, and what they declare), and the gate hands the
84	worker the changed participants as `targets`.
85	
86	**This pack's tasks need the fleet executor routine — a second routine, only in this repo.** Both
87	tasks here declare `session_scope: 'fleet'`, so the scheduler files their dispatches under
88	`ready-for-agent-fleet` rather than `ready-for-agent`, and a *distinct* CCR routine runs them: named
89	`Claudinite executor - fleet`, fired by the **`ready-for-agent-fleet`** label event, with sources =
90	this repo **and every participating member** (that cross-repo reach is the whole reason the scope is
91	split, and is exactly what must stay off an ordinary project's `self` executor). Its launcher prompt
92	is the ordinary one **plus the scope word**:
93	
94	```
95	Execute the Claudinite executor: engine/scheduler/executor.md fleet
96	```
97	
98	That last word is load-bearing and easy to lose: `resolve-dispatch.mjs` defaults an unnamed scope to
99	`self`, so a fleet routine whose prompt omits it declines every dispatch with exit `11` and changes
100	nothing. The failure is **silent and permanent** — the session stops without commenting, the
101	scheduler re-arms the issue on its next hourly pass, and the pair repeats forever, so the only
102	symptom is a `ready-for-agent-fleet` issue that keeps getting re-labeled and never runs. Nothing
103	repo-side can catch it: like the per-repo executor routine baselining checks by hand, this routine is
104	CCR config, not a GitHub artifact an Action can see. If promote or discover-packs has quietly stopped
105	producing anything, read the routine's prompt first.
106	
107	The session-scoped sibling of this nightly lifecycle — mining a single working session for lessons
108	— lives with [the growth pack's extract-from-conversations skill](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md)
109	(applied by the conversation half of its growth-extract daily task over captured logs), and the
110	member-side method docs (extract, dedup, pack discovery, and how a project's local packs are
111	identified) live with [grow_with_claudinite](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md).

How a repo's recurring Claudinite work runs (per-project-scheduling
[DESIGN](../../docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md), issue #394). A repo
schedules **itself**, and the machinery is **three responsibilities, strictly
separated** (owner, 2026-08-06):

  bound is best-effort: the executor surfaces it into the subagent's brief ("fail

input.body:
Weekly `prose-to-checks-sweep` run (dispatched by #712). Scope swept: `.claudinite/local/packs` and `packs` — one conversion.

## The rule converted

From `.claudinite/local/packs/claudinite/RULES.md`:

> …And the pointer cannot go the other way: `docs/` is outside the vendor set, so a link from any file under `packs/` resolves to nothing in every consumer — the `reference-integrity` class that reached `main` unnoticed in #424 (and that check is work-scoped, so it only sees paths the branch itself deletes). Reference `docs/` from the issue or PR instead.

Always-testable (a Markdown link target is a static signature in the artifact), a working rule rather than a product statement, and nothing in the existing catalog covers it — `reference-integrity` only sees paths the branch itself deletes, and `docs/` is never deleted.

## What landed

- **`pack-no-docs-link`** (blocking, world scope) in the `canon-curation` local pack — policing the `packs/` tree is that pack's declared turf, and its home-only declaration gates the rule for free. It resolves each Markdown link target relative to its file and fires when the result lands under `docs/`.
- Scope is the shared canon only: `packs/<pack>/…`, the tree a vendor walk actually carries. `packs/README.md` (root of the tree, outside every pack directory) and the home's own local packs are never vendored, so their `docs/` links resolve for their only reader and stay quiet.
- **See-it-fail fixture** (`pack-docs-link.test.mjs`, 7 cases): fires on a violating pack file; silent on the remedy the finding prescribes (naming the doc without linking), on an in-tree link between packs, on a pack's own `docs/` subdirectory, on `packs/README.md`, on a local pack, and on an external URL whose path merely contains `docs/`. Verified red-first by neutering the detection — the violating case is the only one that fails.

## Live violations it found (fixed here)

| File | Was |
|---|---|
| `packs/basics/scheduled-tasks.md` ×3 | links to `docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md`, `…/MIGRATION.md`, `docs/task-prework/DESIGN.md` |
| `packs/product-wiki/README.md` | link to `docs/per-project-scheduling/DESIGN.md` — repointed at `packs/basics/scheduled-tasks.md`, which is vendored |

Each dangled in every consumer that declares `basics` or `product-wiki`.

## Deletion test

Applied to the paragraph the check now stands beside — **it stays whole**. It carries a second rule in the same breath ("an idea nobody can act on belongs in `docs/`", i.e. out of injected pack prose), which is judgment no check can carry. Per the skill, a paragraph carrying something the check does not is not trimmed.

## Noted, not converted

The same dangling class reaches beyond `docs/`: several pack files link to `engine/checks/DESIGN.md`, `vendoring/DESIGN.md`, `bootstrap.md`, `extending.md` and other canon-root paths that the vendor set also drops (only `engine/scheduler/executor.md` and `engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md` are whitelisted `.md` under `engine/`). That is ~40 links across the tree — a sweep of its own, not this run's bounded surface. This check deliberately covers only the `docs/` rule the prose states.

## Verification

- `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')` — 1341 tests, 0 failures (the new file committed first, so it is actually in the list).
- `node engine/checks/check_the_world.mjs` — 0 blocking, 17 advisory (all pre-existing `file-placement` / `task-phase-discipline`).
- `packs/README.md` corpus tally recomputed from the catalog: 80 → 81; `packs-tests/catalog-tally.test.mjs` green.

Refs #712
